opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, when I started TVM, I didn't have much background in architecture or compilers at all. My training was really in machine learning. I'd built XGBoost and worked on MXNet, so I came at it from the systems-for-ML side, not as someone who had spent years on compiler theory or hardware design.

So in a sense the risk was very real. I was stepping into a field where people had decades of accumulated knowledge, and I was somewhat of an outsider. But I think that was also part of what made it possible. I didn't carry the assumptions of how things "should" be done. What I saw was a very concrete problem: we had all these deep learning frameworks, and a growing number of hardware backends: GPUs, mobile CPUs, and new accelerators. Every combination required a lot of hand-written, hand-tuned kernels. That clearly wasn't going to scale. So the question was simply, can we automate this?

The way I thought about risk was less "do I have the right credentials" and more "is this problem important, and will I learn something even if it doesn't fully work?" I was a PhD student, so the downside was fairly limited. If it failed, I would still come out understanding compilers and hardware much better. And the upside, if it worked, was that it could change how people deploy machine learning.

I also learned a lot by just building and by working with people who knew more than me. I was fortunate to be at the University of Washington, where I could talk with folks in architecture and programming languages. I borrowed a lot of ideas, Halide's separation of algorithm and schedule for example, and then thought about what changes when the workload is deep learning and you can use machine learning itself to search the optimization space.

So my approach was: learn as you go, stay close to real problems, build something people can actually use, and open-source it so the community can tell you quickly whether you're on the right track. That feedback loop was what reduced the risk more than anything else.

r002.rationale: It says he learned about compilers and hardware through building and collaboration, but does not state that the ability to design technical architectures develops through experience.

r003.rationale: The response mentions his prior machine-learning systems work, but does not say that it increased his confidence that TVM was technically feasible.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, when we started TVM, I didn't really think of it in terms of risk, at least not the way people usually frame it. I came from the machine learning side first. I had built XGBoost, I was working on MXNet, and I kept hitting the same wall over and over: every time we wanted to run a model on a new piece of hardware, or try a new operator, somebody had to go hand-write kernels. And that somebody was often me or one of my friends. So the pain was very concrete. It wasn't an abstract bet on compilers being the future, it was more like, "I'm tired of doing this manually, and I don't think it scales."

Now, the honest part is that I was not a compiler person by training. I had taken courses, I knew the basics, but I had never built a production compiler. And I think that was actually both the risk and the advantage. The risk is obvious: compilers are a field with decades of history, LLVM, Halide, polyhedral stuff, and there's a good chance you reinvent something badly. The advantage was that I came in with a very specific problem, deep learning workloads, and I wasn't attached to how things "should" be done. Halide was a huge inspiration, for example, with the separation of algorithm and schedule, and I was happy to borrow those ideas rather than invent everything from scratch.

So the way I managed it was mostly by surrounding myself with people who knew what I didn't. Luis Ceze on the architecture side, Carlos Guestrin, folks like Thierry Moreau who were building actual hardware. If you're going to target hardware, you'd better sit next to people who design hardware. That collaboration, where the compiler people and the architecture people and the ML people were all in the same room, that's really what made it work. Any one of us alone probably would have failed.

And then there's the question of whether anyone would care. At the time, most people thought frameworks plus vendor libraries like cuDNN were enough. I think the bet, if there was one, was that hardware diversity was only going to grow, and that nobody, not even NVIDIA, could hand-optimize everything forever. That turned out to be right faster than I expected. But I'll admit, in the early days it mostly felt like a research project that happened to be useful, not a calculated risk. We open-sourced it early, got feedback from real users, and the project kind of pulled us forward from there.

r001.rationale: He says he did not think of building TVM in terms of risk, at least not in the usual way.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that architecture-design ability can be developed through experience.

r003.rationale: His prior ML work explains the problem motivating TVM, but he does not say it made him more confident TVM was technically feasible to build.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest risk was that I didn’t have a very deep background in either computer architecture or compilers at the time. So there was a lot I needed to learn, and I couldn’t be sure that the approach would work.

But I also felt that the problem was worth exploring. You have these machine learning workloads, and you want to run them efficiently on different hardware. Rather than assuming we could solve the whole problem, we could start with a small piece, build something, and see what we learned. That was how I thought about the risk: not as one big decision where you have to know everything in advance, but as a sequence of experiments.

sol-6.1.text:
At the time, I didn’t think of it as one big bet where we had to know everything before starting. We saw a problem that seemed worth working on: machine learning models were evolving quickly, and there were many different hardware backends. How could we make it easier to bring those two things together?

Of course, there was a lot we didn’t know. Having some background in compilers and architecture helped us formulate the questions, but it didn’t mean we already had the answers. The way to reduce that risk was to build something, see where it worked, and learn from the places where it didn’t.

I think that’s an important part of research. You need a direction you believe in, but you also need to be willing to change your approach as you learn. You don’t have to resolve all the uncertainty before taking the first step.
